record_reviews.summary: Darwin postpones a visit to Monday and sends the Horner family a piece of wedding cake from Shrewsbury, with a request for a piece in return.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 9 August 1837; the date is a preserved single-day metadata value.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The body is Darwin’s signed note. Footnote 1 reports Leonard Horner’s later account of visits, but that reported voice is editorial context, not body prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The visit and cake exchange are personal logistics; no incoming letter or Darwin response prompt is preserved.

evidence.quote: Will you allow me to say Monday
the accompanying segment of cake, which I received from Shrewsbury this morning

record_reviews.summary: Leonard Horner postpones a meeting because he must attend the House of Commons for the Factory Amendment Act and proposes Wednesday instead.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 7 April [1838]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Leonard Horner is the incoming writer; the footnote about Darwin using remaining pages for marriage notes is editorial, not a second voice.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The later uncertain note may be addressed to Leonard Horner, but its volcanic-island subject and suspect transmission do not identify it as a response to this 1838 scheduling letter.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a scheduling postponement with no surviving Darwin reply in the packet.

evidence.quote: This obliges me to postpone the pleasure of your company
I hope Wednesday will suit you equally well

record_reviews.summary: Charlotte Langton warmly congratulates Darwin on his forthcoming marriage and says she will share her pleasure with Emma.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 14 November [1838]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Charlotte Langton writes the body; references to Emma are reported family context, not Darwin voice.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The later Langton letter also concerns Emma and the marriage, but it is another incoming letter and no Darwin response is preserved between them.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Congratulatory social correspondence has no surviving Darwin response in this packet.

evidence.quote: how truly & warmly I rejoice in this marriage
I shall be eager for the next letters

record_reviews.summary: Charlotte Langton thanks Darwin for his letter, reports meeting Emma, and describes Emma’s welcome into the family.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 4 December [1838]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Charlotte Langton writes the body. Her statements about Emma’s reception report Langton’s experience and do not establish a Darwin-authored reply.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The body explicitly thanks an unlocated Darwin letter; that antecedent is not one of the packet’s outgoing records.

evidence.quote: thank you for your letter
it was delightful to be able to meet her here

record_reviews.summary: Darwin, writing for the Geological Society, acknowledges Jukes’s letter, reports the Council’s position on Newfoundland, recommends Sedgwick, and appends a Governor Prescott extract.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 6 December 1838.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes in the Geological Society’s institutional voice. The Governor Prescott passage is an embedded extract and must not be attributed to Darwin.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both Darwin letters concern Jukes’s Newfoundland application, but 461 is a later independent update and does not refer to 453 or repeat its Council acknowledgment.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The acknowledged Jukes letter is absent; the later Jukes-directed letter is not a reply to this institutional dispatch.

evidence.quote: I have been directed by the Council of the Geological Society to acknowledge the receipt of your letter
I have added an extract from the letter of Governor Prescott

record_reviews.summary: Darwin updates Jukes on the Newfoundland application, Sedgwick and Lyell, and offers geological and surveying advice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 25 December [1838]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; references to Lyell and Sedgwick report their separate communications. The Geological Society application and Sedgwick letter are external antecedents.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The shared Jukes/Newfoundland topic does not make this a reply to 453: 461 supplies a later application update and advice, without referring to the earlier Council letter.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jukes application and the Sedgwick communication are mentioned but not preserved as incoming bodies in this packet.

evidence.quote: no application, besides yours, has been received by the Geological Soc.
I have received a letter on the subject of your application from Professor Sedgwick

record_reviews.summary: Fitton thanks Darwin for Journal of researches and praises its geology and unpretentious presentation.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 13 June 1839.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: William Henry Fitton writes the body. His praise of Darwin’s book is Fitton’s voice, and no Darwin response is included.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The 1842 Darwin extract is addressed to Fitton and discusses glacial work, but it does not acknowledge this 1839 book-thanks letter and survives only through secondary transmission.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Fitton’s thanks identify a received Darwin book, not a surviving incoming prompt for an outgoing packet letter.

evidence.quote: I ought long since to have thanked you for your Book
your Geology seems to me to be excellent

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Miller to reduce or publish Sulivan’s Falkland meteorological observations and offers to obtain further answers or material.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 22 November [1839]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body. Sulivan’s observations and willingness to help are reported by Darwin, not an incoming Sulivan or Miller voice.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The later Miller letter is still Darwin-to-Miller and concerns specimens and a Society meeting; no text connects it to these meteorological observations.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The meteorological material is Darwin’s proposal based on Sulivan’s records; no Miller reply is preserved.

evidence.quote: A friend of mine Lieut. Sulivan R.N. has lately surveyed the Falkland Islands
should you like to publish anywhere you choose & reduce these observations

record_reviews.summary: Darwin supplies Gray with a testimonial for the British Museum zoological keeper position.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 1 January [1840]; year is established editorially from Gray’s appointment, not by an exact body date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes a testimonial for Gray. The verso draft mentioned in footnote 4 is Gray’s reported draft, not part of the preserved Darwin body.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both are Darwin letters to Gray about institutional matters, but 660F is a 1843 specimen-loan request and does not answer this testimonial.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Gray incoming letter or explicit response to the testimonial is preserved.

evidence.quote: I have invariably received, when visiting the British Museum the greatest attention from you
would give you strong claims to hold the situation

record_reviews.summary: Darwin apologises for retaining the Royal Geographical Society’s Krusenstern atlas, locates Sulphur Island and related chart features, and offers to return or replace the atlas.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single editorially supplied day, 7 January [1840]; footnote dates it in the context of Hall’s sixth edition, while Hall’s request itself is not preserved.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body. The geological claims are his own analysis of Hall’s described observations; no Hall wording is present in the packet.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The March letter is another Darwin letter to Hall on a different Coquimbo/Glen Roy question; the shared recipient does not establish that it replies to this atlas-location note.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The body answers Hall’s unlocated request about chart positions; no Hall incoming letter or distinct response prompt is preserved.

evidence.quote: I am sorry that I have caused you any inconvenience by having Krusentern’s atlas in my possession.
I have an indistinct recollection that this isld was formerly called Sulphur isld

record_reviews.summary: Darwin gives Hall a second detailed discussion of Coquimbo, Patagonia, and Glen Roy, while noting illness and the absence of Hall’s work at hand.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 15 March 1840.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body. Footnotes report Hall’s later publication and the absent Hall letter; those reports are editorial evidence, not additional body voices.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Although the two Darwin letters share Hall and Coquimbo/Glen Roy, 558F has no explicit reference to 550 and the editorial record says Hall’s initiating letter is missing; treat them as separate responses to an unlocated prompt.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The editorial footnote expressly says no letter from Hall has been found; the surviving body is not enough to identify a direct predecessor.

evidence.quote: If the valley be considered as bounded by the mountains of granitic rocks its width is between 3 & 4 miles.
traces of ‘Parallel Roads’ have been discovered in other parts of Scotland

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s Gardeners’ Chronicle contribution reports humble-bees boring flower corollas and considers whether hive-bees acquire the practice by imitation.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Draft dated 16 August 1841; publication date 21 August 1841.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin’s contribution is preserved as a printed letter/article. The editorial footnotes and publication context are not Darwin body voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a published natural-history contribution, not a response to a surviving incoming letter in the packet.

evidence.quote: Perhaps some of your readers may like to hear a few more particulars about the humble-bees which bore holes in flowers
it will, I think, be a very instructive case of acquired knowledge in insects

record_reviews.summary: A transmitted extract from a Darwin letter to Fitton describes glacial observations in North Wales and Darwin’s revised view of Glen Roy.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 23 June 1842, but the packet preserves an excerpt copied from a Darwin letter rather than the original letter.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The excerpt is attributed to Darwin by the editorial record, but its transmission through Fitton/Buckland/Agassiz is reporting/copyist context; do not treat the enclosing correspondent’s voice as Darwin’s.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Fitton is the recipient in both records, but the 1842 extract’s glacial content does not answer Fitton’s 1839 book thanks and the original is not preserved.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The original Darwin-to-Fitton letter and any Fitton prompt are absent; the excerpt cannot establish a direct pair.

evidence.quote: Yesterday (and the previous days) I had some most interesting work in examining the marks left by extinct glaciers
I am also, more convinced that the valleys of Glen Roy

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks the Horner family for congratulations, reports Emma’s recovery, and comments on Leonard Horner’s illness and praise for Coral reefs.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 4 October [1842]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body. The letter from Lyell and the Horner family’s incoming letter are reported references, not preserved packet records.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The opening thanks an unlocated Horner letter; no surviving Horner response or prompt target is in this packet.

evidence.quote: I am very much obliged for your letter & most kind congratulations from yourself & Mr. Horner & Katharine
I have received such a letter from Lyell on my Coral Volume

record_reviews.summary: Darwin responds to Julian Jackson’s proposed review of Coral reefs and leaves the publication venue to Jackson’s judgment.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 13 October [1842]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body to Julian Jackson. Jackson’s proposed review is referenced but his initiating communication is not preserved in the packet.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 672 is a later Darwin letter to the Royal Geographical Society concerning Jackson’s offer; shared addressee context does not make it a reply to 650.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This answers an unlocated Jackson proposal about reviewing Coral reefs; no incoming review request is preserved.

evidence.quote: your intention of drawing up a short account of my volume, as a very great compliment
I hope you will turn it in your own mind, & decide whichever is most agreeable to yourself

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Miller about geological specimens needed for his notes and urges attendance at a Geological Society meeting.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Bounded writing range, 16 October–27 November 1842; the body’s Sunday heading and meeting reference do not collapse the editorial range to one day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body. Miller’s earlier specimen examination is referred to, but no Miller response is preserved.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both are Darwin-to-Miller letters, but 651 concerns geological specimens and a December Society meeting rather than 546’s Sulivan meteorology; they are not a direct pair.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The specimen exchanges are referred to retrospectively and the requested Miller answer is absent.

evidence.quote: I am finally preparing for press some of my geological notes
ought if they possibly can to attend the Special general meeting on December 3d

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers Maclaren’s three objections to Coral reefs, especially the problem of thin elevated limestones, and defends his denudation argument.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Bounded writing range, 15 November–December 1842; the editorial date depends on Maclaren’s review/publication context and remains a range.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the response. Maclaren’s objections are summarized in editorial footnotes and answered by Darwin; the review is a published text, not a packet incoming letter.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 661 is a later marginal postscript asking for return of the annotated pamphlet; it is not the incoming review prompt or a response to this long letter.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The antecedent is Maclaren’s published review, while no letter from Maclaren prompting this response is preserved.

evidence.quote: Your third objection appears to me much the most, indeed the only, formidable one
Your third criticism strikes me as a very weighty and perplexing one

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Gray to seek trustees’ permission for Lyell to borrow Darwin’s coral-reef specimens for lectures.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 25 January [1843]; year is editorially established from the lecture context.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body to Gray. Footnote 4 reports a Gray draft on the verso, but that reported/request-forwarding text is not part of the Darwin body read here.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both are Darwin-to-Gray institutional letters, but this specimen-loan request is separated by years and does not answer the earlier testimonial.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The trustees’ decision and Gray’s verso draft are external to the surviving Darwin body; no incoming response is preserved.

evidence.quote: Mr Lyell is going to give as you are aware some lectures on Geology
lay the request before the Trustees

record_reviews.summary: A pencil postscript on Maclaren’s annotated Coral reefs review asks Maclaren to return the pamphlet.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Approximate range, c. February 1843; the date is inferred from Maclaren’s publication sequence and remains conditional.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: This is Darwin’s pencil postscript on an annotated pamphlet, not a conventional letter body. Maclaren’s review is the object addressed, but the note is not a preserved incoming correspondence prompt.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both concern Maclaren’s Coral reefs review, but 661 is a return request on the pamphlet and neither text explicitly identifies the other as an exchange pair.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The note is a material-return request attached to a publication; no separate incoming Maclaren letter is preserved.

evidence.quote: Wd you be so kind sometime to return me this

record_reviews.summary: Hinds answers Darwin’s queries about Clipperton, Cocos, Cactornis, Bow Island depth, and Pacific coral formations, with explicit cautions about observation.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 21 April 1843.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Richard Brinsley Hinds writes the body in response to Darwin’s unlocated queries. The references to Belcher, Gould and Pritchard report their views, not Darwin voice.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 683 is a later Hinds follow-up about Cactornis, but it does not quote or explicitly answer 671; its footnote points back to 671 while both are incoming to Darwin.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Hinds explicitly says he is replying to Darwin’s 9 April queries, which are absent from the packet.

evidence.quote: replying to your queries contained in your letter of the 9th. Inst
I must request you to take them with caution

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Julian Jackson for offering to put him forward for the Royal Geographical Society Council but declines because attendance would take too much time.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 23 April [1843]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes to the Royal Geographical Society about Jackson’s offer. Jackson’s offer is reported by Darwin and no incoming offer letter is preserved.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 650 is an earlier Darwin letter to Jackson about Coral reefs review; 672 concerns Society Council service and has no textual connection to the review.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The offer to put Darwin on the Council list is unlocated; it is not evidence that Darwin read a surviving Jackson letter.

evidence.quote: Thank you for your obliging offer of putting me on the list for the Council of the Geographical Soc
coming up to town robs me of so much time

record_reviews.summary: An uncertain copy or possible forgery, addressed to an unidentified recipient, says Darwin sent notes on Volcanic islands for inspection and return.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 25 June 1843 in the page metadata, but the editorial note says the address and wording may reflect an inaccurate copy or forgery.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Voice attribution is unresolved: the page catalogues it as Darwin, while the editorial note identifies possible copyist interpolation/forgery and an uncertain addressee. Do not use it as a secure Darwin witness.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The possible Leonard Horner identity is not enough to connect this 1843 volcanic-island note to Horner’s 1838 scheduling letter; the subject, transmission and addressee remain uncertain.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The original source and secure addressee are unavailable, so no direct reply or knowledge edge is justified.

evidence.quote: I have sent you the notes on Volcanic Islands for your inspection when you have read them kindly return them to me

record_reviews.summary: Hinds tells Darwin that Gould obtained a Cactornis specimen and that Hinds recognises it as native to Bow Island.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single dated day, 19 July [1843]; bracketed year is editorially supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Richard Brinsley Hinds writes the body. Footnote 1 points to Hinds’s 21 April letter, but editorial cross-reference is not itself a Darwin receipt or an exact claim that 683 answers 671.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 683’s “Soon after the receipt of your note” and the footnote to 671 support a possible Hinds continuation, but the intervening Darwin note is missing and 683 does not say it answers 671.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The letter refers to Darwin’s note and is cross-referenced to 671, but the intervening prompt and the exact relation to 671 are not preserved.

evidence.quote: Soon after the receipt of your note Mr Gould obtained from the Zoological Society a species of Cactornis
you will be gratified to learn that I recognize it as a native of Bow Island

record_reviews.summary: Darwin submits Gentiana specimens and a cabbage-leaf to the Gardeners’ Chronicle, arguing that environmental sterility may cause double flowers; the printed text contains editorial insertions noted separately.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Bounded date, late August 1843; the item was printed in the Gardeners’ Chronicle and its editorial additions must remain distinct from Darwin’s submission.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the preserved letter text. Footnote 3 identifies an editor’s interpolation in paragraph 2 and footnote 5 another insertion; those inserted words are not Darwin voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a publication submission with specimens and a botanical hypothesis; no incoming editor/correspondent prompt is preserved.

evidence.quote: The inclosed specimens appear to me curious, as in some degree connected with the origin of double flowers
You state in your “Theory of Horticulture,” that the origin of double flowers is not well understood

proposed_links.reason: The later Hinds letter is editorially cross-referenced to 671 and says it followed receipt of a Darwin note, but it does not identify 671 as the prompt; the missing intervening Darwin note could be the actual prompt. Both surviving records are Hinds-to-Darwin, so this cannot establish Darwin receipt or a Darwin-authored response.
proposed_links.response_scope: Cactornis result only; relation to the earlier Hinds answer is unresolved

evidence.quote: replying to your queries contained in your letter of the 9th. Inst
Soon after the receipt of your note Mr Gould obtained from the Zoological Society a species of Cactornis

unlocated_references.description: Jukes’s acknowledged letter and the missing Government/Society response chain are not preserved in this packet.
Jukes’s application and the Sedgwick communication referred to by Darwin are absent.
Hall’s question and description of Coquimbo, identified by the editorial notes as the prompt, are absent.
The editorial notes state that no letter from Hall has been found; the initiating Hall request is unavailable.
The original Darwin-to-Fitton letter is absent; only a copied extract transmitted through Buckland/Agassiz survives.
The Horner family letter for which Darwin gives thanks is not in this packet.
Jackson’s proposed-review communication is referred to but not preserved.
Miller’s earlier specimen return/examination correspondence is referred to but not preserved.
Darwin’s 9 April query letter, explicitly answered by Hinds, is absent.
Jackson’s offer to nominate Darwin for the Council list is reported but not preserved.
The Darwin note received by Hinds before the Cactornis result is absent; it may be the prompt rather than 671.

date_sections.basis: Editorial range and Sunday heading; no exact day inferred from the 3 December meeting reference.
Editorial dating from Maclaren’s review/publication sequence; not collapsed to the publication date.
Conditional dating from publication chronology of Maclaren’s pamphlet; remains approximate.
Editorial publication/draft dating; no exact day inferred.

issues: No packet record establishes a Darwin-authored direct reply to any of the five incoming items; incoming dates are not treated as receipt dates.
453 includes an embedded Governor Prescott extract, and 660F’s footnote reports a Gray verso draft; neither reported voice is treated as Darwin body prose.

550 is an atlas-location note and 558F is the separate Coquimbo/Glen Roy discussion; both are Darwin-to-Hall items with Hall’s prompts missing, so same recipient does not establish an inter-letter reply.
632 is a copied extract, not the full original Darwin letter; 607 and 693 are printed Gardeners’ Chronicle submissions, with 693 editorial insertions kept separate.
677 has unresolved copyist/forgery and addressee concerns and is not used for a secure edge.
683→671 remains only a candidate continuation/reference; a missing intervening Darwin note may be the actual prompt.
